```{r}
#| label: setup

library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)

# Must match EXPERIMENT.id in experiment.js, and the --experiment you passed to the export.
# Phase 2 runs under its own id, so its data never mix with Phase 1's.
experiment_id        <- "zeelenberg1996-pilot-b"
experiment_id_phase2 <- "zeelenberg1996-phase2"
# Pilot B, reported in Methods. Kept separate so that section still shows Pilot B after
# experiment_id moves to the final study.

```

```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. Replace these with your original study's
# values, and say in a comment exactly where in the paper each one comes from.
#
# Zeelenberg et al. (1996), Experiment 1 (pp. 151-152 and Figure 1): 78 psychology
# undergraduates (26 per feedback condition). Number who chose the risky gamble (R), read
# from Figure 1 (p. 152); the text gives the test statistics but none of the counts:
# - risky feedback 16 of 26 (10 chose S), choice only 11 of 26 (15), safe feedback 6 of 26 (20).
# - These counts reproduce every reported test: key test chi2(1) = 7.88, p < .005; all three
#   conditions chi2(2) = 7.88, p < .02; each feedback condition vs choice only 1.93 and 2.18.
original <- tibble(
  condition = c("risky_feedback", "choice_only", "safe_feedback"),
  n         = c(26, 26, 26),
  risky     = c(16, 11, 6)
)
original_p_risky <- with(original, risky[condition == "risky_feedback"] / n[condition == "risky_feedback"])
original_p_safe  <- with(original, risky[condition == "safe_feedback"] / n[condition == "safe_feedback"])

# Other statistics the original reports, for the secondary analyses (p. 152).
original_secondary <- list(
  # Mean matched X, in Dutch guilders; this replication uses the same numbers in dollars
  # (f130 -> $130). No difference between conditions, F(2, 75) < 0.3.
  matched_x_mean = 69.05,
  # Attractiveness ratings (1-12): R 6.71 vs S 7.41, t(77) = -3.27, p < .01.
  attract_r_mean = 6.71,
  attract_s_mean = 7.41,
  # Risk preference, (+1 risky / -1 safe) x (strength - 0.5): F(2, 75) = 3.46, p < .05;
  # risky vs safe feedback t(75) = -2.63, p < .01; linear trend F = 6.90, p < .01; each feedback
  # condition vs choice only t(75) = 1.19 and 1.44, ns, listed in the opposite order to what the
  # means imply (risky vs choice only 1.44, safe vs choice only 1.19).
  risk_pref_means = c(risky_feedback = 0.88, choice_only = -1.73, safe_feedback = -3.88)
)

# Order and labels for the three feedback conditions in tables and figures.
condition_labels <- c(risky_feedback = "Risky feedback",
                      choice_only    = "Choice only",
                      safe_feedback  = "Safe feedback")
```

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Short notes in the rendered report, e.g. "not enough data yet". This Quarto version does not
# show message() output, so notes are printed as ordinary output instead.
note <- function(...) cat(paste0(...), "\n")

# Exclusion settings.
# Screens that need an answer. Finishing one of them faster than this is not humanly possible
# (the screen alone takes 150 ms to fade in), so it marks an automated response.
min_screen_ms <- 300
answer_tasks  <- c("matching", "attractiveness", "comprehension", "choice",
                   "preference_strength", "reasons", "regret_scale", "end_survey")
# Proof of Human bot-risk score (0-100) at or above which a participant is excluded as a likely
# bot: 50, the start of the vendor's "review" band, chosen after Pilot B (no completer scored
# above 15). NA would report scores without excluding anyone. Participants with no score (the
# tracker was blocked or failed to load) are kept and counted.
poh_exclude_at <- 50

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()
  # Bot-risk scores, written by scripts/poh-scores.js after the export (NULL until then).
  poh_path <- file.path(dir, "poh.csv")
  poh <- if (file.exists(poh_path)) read_csv(poh_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL

  # Every participant document is one page load, including visits that never consented. Someone
  # who clicks "I do not agree" also reaches the end of the study (completed = TRUE), so a
  # completer must have consented too.
  consented_ids <- trials |> filter(task == "consent", consented %in% TRUE) |> pull(participant_id)
  complete <- participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE, participant_id %in% consented_ids)

  # Exclusion 1, repeat sessions. The export links each person's sessions (by Prolific ID, or by
  # browser when there is none) and flags them. Keep each person's first completed session, and
  # exclude the person if an earlier session had already reached the feedback instructions:
  # they may have read another condition's feedback rule.
  has_repeat_flags <- all(c("earlier_completed", "earlier_saw_feedback") %in% names(participants))
  repeat_ids <- if (has_repeat_flags) {
    complete |> filter(earlier_completed %in% TRUE | earlier_saw_feedback %in% TRUE) |> pull(participant_id)
  } else character(0)

  # Exclusion 2, impossibly fast answers: any answer screen finished in under min_screen_ms.
  too_fast_ids <- trials |>
    filter(task %in% answer_tasks, participant_id %in% complete$participant_id,
           as.numeric(rt) < min_screen_ms) |>
    distinct(participant_id) |> pull(participant_id)

  # Exclusion 3, likely bots: a bot-risk score at or above poh_exclude_at. No score is no
  # evidence either way, so those participants are kept.
  bot_ids <- if (!is.null(poh) && !is.na(poh_exclude_at)) {
    poh |> filter(participant_id %in% complete$participant_id, risk_score >= poh_exclude_at) |>
      pull(participant_id)
  } else character(0)

  keep <- complete |> filter(!participant_id %in% c(repeat_ids, too_fast_ids, bot_ids))

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors, poh = poh,
       consented_ids = consented_ids, complete = complete, keep = keep,
       has_repeat_flags = has_repeat_flags, repeat_ids = repeat_ids, too_fast_ids = too_fast_ids,
       bot_ids = bot_ids)
}

# The key comparison's raw counts: how many analysed participants chose the risky gamble (R)
# in each feedback condition.
risky_counts <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(risky = sum(choice == "risky"), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# The key statistic: difference in the proportion choosing the risky gamble (risky feedback
# minus safe feedback) with a 95% CI, and the uncorrected chi-square, which is the same test
# (and reproduces the original's chi2(1) = 7.88). NULL until both conditions have at least one
# analysed participant.
diff_ci <- function(counts) {
  rf <- counts[counts$condition == "risky_feedback", ]
  sf <- counts[counts$condition == "safe_feedback", ]
  if (nrow(rf) == 0 || nrow(sf) == 0) return(NULL)
  pt <- suppressWarnings(prop.test(c(rf$risky, sf$risky), c(rf$n, sf$n), correct = FALSE))
  tibble(N = rf$n + sf$n,
         estimate = unname(pt$estimate[1] - pt$estimate[2]),
         ci_low = pt$conf.int[1], ci_high = pt$conf.int[2],
         statistic = unname(pt$statistic), p = pt$p.value)
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given.
prop_ci <- function(x, n) {
  ci <- suppressWarnings(prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE))$conf.int
  tibble(p = x / n, low = ci[1], high = ci[2])
}
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    rowwise() |> mutate(prop_ci(risky, n)) |> ungroup() |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           condition = factor(unname(condition_labels[condition]), levels = condition_labels),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8, preserve = "single")
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = p, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    # n labels sit inside the bar in white, or in dark grey when the bar is too short to hold them.
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label, colour = p >= 0.07, group = Study), position = dodge,
              vjust = 0, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey25")) +
    scale_x_discrete(drop = FALSE) +   # keep all three conditions, even one with no pilot data
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Feedback condition", y = "Chose the risky gamble (R)", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r, missing = "not yet collected") {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (risky − safe feedback)` = missing,
                  `95% CI` = "", `χ²(1)` = "", p = ""))
  }
  # With very few participants (e.g. Pilot A) the test can be undefined; show a dash.
  num <- function(x, fmt) if (is.finite(x)) sprintf(fmt, x) else "-"
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (risky − safe feedback)` = sprintf("%.0f points", 100 * r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * r$ci_low, 100 * r$ci_high),
         `χ²(1)` = num(r$statistic, "%.2f"),
         p = if (is.finite(r$p)) format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001) else "-")
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", diff_ci(original)),
  # With data but nobody yet in one of the two key conditions, say so rather than "not yet collected".
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) diff_ci(risky_counts(phase1)),
          if (have_data) "needs participants in both key conditions" else "not yet collected"),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) diff_ci(risky_counts(phase2)),
          if (have_phase2) "needs participants in both key conditions" else "not yet collected")
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrlllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: difference in the percentage of analysed participants choosing the risky gamble, risky-feedback minus safe-feedback condition.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

<!--
"What if the other option would have turned out better?" Regret depends
on being able to answer that question. If I never learn how the path I
passed up would have gone, I have nothing to compare my outcome against,
and so nothing to regret. Some decisions hide that answer, and others
reveal it whether I want it or not, and people can therefore protect
themselves from regret without being more cautious, simply by choosing
the option that keeps the alternative out of view.

Zeelenberg et al. (1996) used this idea to challenge the view that
anticipated regret makes people cautious. Experiment 1 separated
avoiding risk and avoiding regret by telling participants in advance
which of two gambles would have its outcome revealed regardless of their
choice. Participants followed the feedback, not the risk: most chose the
risky gamble when its outcome would always be shown, and few did when
the safe gamble's outcome would be. I replicated this comparison. It
matters for my research on regret and agency, where I study how people
delegate decisions and how it impacts outcome ownership and regret.

To run the study, I built its procedure in jsPsych and recruited on
Prolific. After adjusting a safe gamble to be as attractive as a risky
one, participants learned which gamble's outcome they would see
regardless of their choice: the risky one, the safe one, or only the one
they chose. They then chose a gamble, rated the strength of their
preference, and wrote their reasons. Not having the exact feedback
instructions that were presumably in Dutch originally made it harder to
replicate. The key test was a chi-square test of gamble choice by
feedback condition, comparing risky feedback with safe feedback
(original: 16 of 26 versus 6 of 26 chose the risky gamble, χ²(1) = 7.88,
p \< .005). A possible extension would add a comprehension check on the
feedback instruction and test in another domain that is not gambling
related.

--> 

"What if the other option would have turned out better?" Regret as an emotion depends on being able to answer this question: when a decision maker never learns how the forgone option would have turned out, there is nothing to compare the outcome against, and therefore nothing to regret. Zeelenberg et al. (1996) used this idea to challenge the view that anticipated regret makes people risk averse. Experiment 1, which I replicated, separated avoiding risk and avoiding regret by telling participants in advance which of two gambles would have its outcome revealed regardless of their choice. Choices tracked the expected feedback rather than the riskiness of the options: most participants chose the risky gamble when its outcome would always be revealed, and few did so when the safe gamble's outcome would be. The finding is relevant to my research on regret and agency, which examines how delegating decisions affects people's sense of ownership over outcomes and the regret they feel about them.

I implemented the procedure in jsPsych and recruited participants on Prolific. Participants first considered two hypothetical gambles: a risky gamble paying \$130 with a 35% chance, and a safe gamble paying \$X with a 65% chance. They entered the value of X that made the two gambles equally attractive to them and were then randomly assigned to one of three feedback conditions. In the risky feedback condition, they would always learn the outcome of the risky gamble; in the safe feedback condition, the outcome of the safe gamble; and in the choice-only condition, only the outcome of the gamble they chose. After a short comprehension quiz on the feedback instruction, participants chose a gamble, rated the strength of their preference, and explained their choice. Because the original feedback instructions were not printed in the paper and were presumably written in Dutch, I wrote new instructions from the paper's description; I also converted the original amounts from Dutch guilders to dollars.

The key test was a chi-square test on the 2 × 2 table of feedback condition (risky vs. safe) by gamble choice; the choice-only condition was not part of this test. In the original study, 16 of 26 participants chose the risky gamble in the risky feedback condition, compared with 6 of 26 in the safe feedback condition, χ²(1) = 7.88, p < .005. A possible extension would make the choice consequential by paying participants a bonus based on the outcome of their chosen gamble, while revealing only the outcomes their condition specified.

## Methods

### Power analysis

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Report the original effect size, the sample needed for 80%, 90% and 95%
power to detect it, and the sample you chose and why. The table below is
computed from the original study's numbers entered at the top of this
file.

Original effects are usually overestimates, so powering to the original
effect tends to produce an underpowered replication. One widely used
alternative is to collect 2.5 times the original sample, which gives 80%
power to detect an effect the original study had only 33% power to
detect (Simonsohn, 2015; Experimentology §10.4). Say which approach you
used, and what the course's participant budget allowed.
:::
-->

```{r}
#| label: power
# Power for the key comparison (risky vs safe feedback). The study has three conditions, so
# the total is three times the per-condition N.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.prop.test(p1 = original_p_safe, p2 = original_p_risky,
                       power = pw, sig.level = 0.05)$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_per_group = ceiling(n),
         n_key = 2 * ceiling(n), n_total = 3 * ceiling(n))
})

original_effect <- original_p_risky - original_p_safe
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original$n)   # per condition, in the order of `original`

# Numbers quoted in the text below: the planned N per condition (2.5 x 26 = 65) and the key
# test's power at that N, for the original effect and for half of it.
n_per_condition <- two_and_half[1]
power_original  <- power.prop.test(n = n_per_condition, p1 = original_p_safe, p2 = original_p_risky)$power
half_effect     <- original_p_safe + original_effect / 2
power_half      <- power.prop.test(n = n_per_condition, p1 = original_p_safe, p2 = half_effect)$power
# Smallest difference (risky minus safe feedback) detectable with 80% power at that N.
min_detectable  <- uniroot(function(p2) power.prop.test(n = n_per_condition, p1 = original_p_safe, p2 = p2)$power - 0.8,
                           c(original_p_safe + 0.01, 0.99))$root - original_p_safe

knitr::kable(power_rows,
             col.names = c("Power", "N per condition", "N in the key comparison (2 conditions)",
                           "N total (3 conditions)"),
             caption = sprintf(
               paste("Sample needed to detect the original effect (risky choice: %.0f%% with risky feedback",
                     "vs %.0f%% with safe feedback, a difference of %.0f points), two-sided alpha = .05.",
                     "For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample is %d per condition, %d in total."),
               100 * original_p_risky, 100 * original_p_safe, 100 * original_effect,
               two_and_half[1], sum(two_and_half)))
```

The original study found a difference of `r round(100 * original_effect)` percentage points in risky choice between the risky and safe feedback conditions. I will follow the 2.5-times rule (Simonsohn, 2015) rather than power the study to the original effect, which gives 80% power to detect an effect the original study had only 33% power to detect. With `r two_and_half[1]` participants per condition, the key test will have `r scales::percent(power_original, accuracy = 0.1)` power to detect the original effect and `r scales::percent(power_half, accuracy = 1)` power to detect half of it (and the smallest difference it can detect with 80% power is `r round(100 * min_detectable)` percentage points).

### Planned sample

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Planned sample size and stopping rule, sampling frame (for example, "US
residents on Prolific, fluent in English, 18 or older"), known
demographics, and any preselection or screening. The stopping rule
should be data-independent: "collect until N participants pass the
exclusion criteria below" rather than "until the result is clear".
:::
-->

```{r}
#| label: budget
# Planned sample and cost. Update minutes after Pilot B (median total_ms in participants.csv)
# and the hourly rate from the Class Prolific Guidelines.
n_total <- sum(two_and_half)        # 195 = 2.5 x the original 78, 65 per condition
minutes <- 6                        # expected study length in minutes (Pilot B median: 5.7)
hourly  <- 9                        # US$ per hour ($0.90 for 6 minutes)
fee     <- 1/3                      # Prolific's service fee on top of pay
cost_paid  <- n_total * minutes / 60 * hourly
cost_total <- cost_paid * (1 + fee)
budget <- tibble(Minutes = minutes,
                 `Pay per person` = minutes / 60 * hourly,
                 `Paid to participants` = cost_paid,
                 `Total with fee` = cost_total)
knitr::kable(budget, digits = 2,
             caption = sprintf("Estimated cost of %d participants for a %d-minute study at $%d per hour, including Prolific's service fee.",
                               n_total, minutes, hourly))
```

I will collect `r sum(two_and_half)` analyzable participants, 2.5 times the original sample of `r sum(original$n)`, or about `r two_and_half[1]` per condition; because assignment is random, the per-condition numbers will be approximate. Participants will be people on Prolific, fluent in English, aged 18 to 25, and using a desktop or laptop computer. I restricted the age range to bring the sample closer to the original's undergraduate participants. I will also use Prolific's quota sampling to recruit equal numbers of men and women. This is my own choice, since the original reports neither the age nor the gender of its participants. At about `r minutes` minutes per participant and `r scales::dollar(hourly)` per hour, including Prolific's service fee, the planned sample will cost about `r scales::dollar(cost_total, accuracy = 1)`.

I will first recruit `r sum(two_and_half)` participants. After applying the exclusion criteria, I will replace each excluded participant with a new participant of the same sex on Prolific's screener, assigned at random like the original batch, and repeat until `r sum(two_and_half)` participants have passed the exclusion criteria. This keeps the sexes as close to equal as possible among the analysed sample; because `r sum(two_and_half)` is odd, the split will be 98 and 97. The number recruited will depend only on the number of exclusions.


### Materials

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

All materials. You can quote the original article directly: put the text
in quotation marks and note that it was followed precisely, or quote it
and point out the exceptions. Link to the live experiment above rather
than pasting screenshots of every screen.
:::
-->

The original questionnaire was never published, so the on-screen text was reconstructed from the paper's description of it (Zeelenberg et al., 1996, pp. 151–152). The paper calls the gambles R and S, and this report keeps those labels; participants, however, see them as Gamble A (risky) and Gamble B (safe), the labels used in the original questionnaire (M. Zeelenberg, personal communication, October 20, 2026). The full study can be taken at the live experiment link above.

| Material | Original | This replication | Exceptions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gambles | "Two hypothetical gambles, gamble R (risky) and gamble S (safe), each of which could result in a positive outcome" (p. 151): f130 with 35%, f0 with 65% (R); fX with 65%, f0 with 35% (S) | Gamble A: "\$130 with 35%", "\$0 with 65%". Gamble B: "\$X with 65%", "\$0 with 35%" | Dollars instead of guilders; labelled A and B instead of R and S, as in the original questionnaire (M. Zeelenberg, personal communication, October 20, 2026) |
| Matching | "Make gamble S exactly as attractive as gamble R ... write down the value of X for which he or she found the gambles equally attractive" (p. 151) | "Make Gamble B exactly as attractive as Gamble A: write down the value of X for which you find the gambles equally attractive." | Added explanation of X below the question, ending with an instruction to click Update X; Gamble B's card shows X after the participant clicks Update X or presses Enter; X must be more than \$0 and less than \$130 (with a message shown only if it is not) |
| Attractiveness | "Rate the attractiveness of each option on a scale ranging from not attractive (1) to very attractive (12)" (p. 151) | Same wording | Buttons instead of paper; the ratings appear only after X is first updated, and changing X afterwards clears them |
| Choice set-up | Participants "learned that, although they had made the gambles equally attractive, they were required to choose between them" (p. 151) | "Although you have made the gambles equally attractive, you are required to choose between them." then "Before you choose, please note:" and the condition's feedback text | Second person |
| Feedback instructions | Described on pp. 151–152; see the next table | See the next table | Reconstructed from the description; shown again on the choice screen |
| Choice | Participants "made the choice (risky or safe gamble)" (p. 152) | Gamble cards and feedback text above "Which gamble do you choose?", with buttons Gamble A and Gamble B | Buttons instead of paper |
| Strength of preference | "On a 12-point scale ranging from weak preference (1) to strong preference (12)" (p. 152) | "You chose Gamble A" (or B), then "Indicate the strength of your preference for the chosen option on a 12-point scale ranging from weak preference (1) to strong preference (12)." | Second person; buttons instead of paper |
| Reasons | "Asked to write down reasons for their choice" (p. 152) | "Write down the reasons for your choice." | Minimum of 30 characters; pasting blocked |

| Condition | The paper's description (pp. 151–152) | On-screen text |
|---|---|---|
| Choice only | "They would only know the outcome of the gamble that they chose, and that they would not be able to compare their outcome with the outcome of the non-chosen gamble" | "You would only know the outcome of the gamble that you choose. You would not be able to compare your outcome with the outcome of the non-chosen gamble." |
| Risky feedback | "They would always know the outcome of the risky gamble and the outcome of the gamble they chose. They also read that they would be able to compare their outcome with the outcome of the non-chosen gamble if they selected gamble S, but not if they selected gamble R" | "You would always know the outcome of Gamble A and the outcome of the gamble you choose. You would be able to compare your outcome with the outcome of the non-chosen gamble if you select Gamble B, but not if you select Gamble A." |
| Safe feedback | Mirrors risky feedback with R and S swapped, but adds "only" ("would only be able to compare") | The risky feedback text with A and B swapped, without the added "only", so the two conditions differ only in the gamble named |

The comprehension quiz is new and checks both the gambles and the feedback rule. If any answer is wrong, participants see "Some of your answers were incorrect. Please read the instructions again."

| Quiz item | Correct answer |
|---|---|
| Chance of winning \$130 with Gamble A | 35% |
| Chance of winning \$X (the participant's own value) with Gamble B | 65% |
| Would you know the outcome of the gamble you choose? | Yes |
| If you choose Gamble A, would you know the outcome of Gamble B? | Yes only in the safe feedback condition |
| If you choose Gamble B, would you know the outcome of Gamble A? | Yes only in the risky feedback condition |

| Added material | Content |
|---|---|
| Consent | The course's approved consent text |
| Welcome | Explains that the gambles are hypothetical: "no real money is involved, but please answer as if it were" |
| Regret Scale (exploratory) | Five items (Schwartz et al., 2002), rated from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree), item 5 reverse-scored |
| End form | How often they gambled in the past 12 months; how much the information about which outcomes they would learn influenced their choice; age, gender, race and ethnicity, each with "Prefer not to say"; an optional feedback box |
| Debrief | What the study tested, and that none of the gambles was played |
| Bot detection | Proof of Human (poh.org) records typing rhythm, mouse movement and scrolling, and checks for virtual machines, VPNs and headless browsers. It produces a risk score from 0 to 100 per session (higher means more likely a bot) and individual checks, such as programmatic typing |

All added materials are identical across conditions.

### Procedure

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

As for Materials: quote the original where you can and point out the
exceptions. Describe the sequence a participant experiences, from
consent to debrief, and how long it takes.
:::
--->

In the original, "participants were seated in separate cubicles and given a questionnaire," and "the experiment used a two-phase procedure" (Zeelenberg et al., 1996, p. 151). Participants were "randomly assigned to one of the three conditions," with 26 in each (p. 151). In this replication, participants will arrive from Prolific, and only desktop and laptop computers will be allowed. Each participant will be randomly assigned, with equal probability, to the choice-only, risky feedback or safe feedback condition when the page loads.

| Step | What happens | Original | Exceptions |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Consent | Course consent text; "I do not agree" ends the study, and "I agree to participate" continues and starts the bot-detection tracker | Not described | Course requirement |
| 2. Welcome | Explains that the gambles are hypothetical, that there are no right or wrong answers, and that the study takes about six minutes in one sitting on a computer | Not described | New |
| 3. Matching and attractiveness | Participants type the value of X that makes the gambles equally attractive and click Update X, which shows it on Gamble B's card; they then rate both gambles from 1 to 12. Changing X clears the ratings, and Continue requires both ratings and an updated X between \$0 and \$130 | Phase 1: "make gamble S exactly as attractive as gamble R" (p. 151); "Next, he or she was asked to rate the attractiveness of each option" (p. 151) | One screen instead of two steps; Update X button; range check; buttons instead of paper |
| 4. Feedback instructions | Participants are told they must choose between the gambles and read their condition's feedback text | Phase 2: "Before they made the choice, however, participants learned about possible feedback on foregone outcomes" (p. 151) | Second person |
| 5. Comprehension quiz | Five questions; if any answer is wrong, participants return to step 4 with a notice and retake the quiz until all five are correct, without being told which was wrong; the number of attempts is recorded | Not in the original | New |
| 6. Choice | Participants see the gambles and feedback text again and click Gamble A or Gamble B | "Participants then made the choice (risky or safe gamble)" (p. 152) | Feedback text repeated; buttons instead of paper |
| 7. Strength of preference | Participants rate the strength of their preference from 1 to 12 | "indicated the strength of their preference for the chosen option" (p. 152) | Buttons instead of paper |
| 8. Reasons | Participants type their reasons, at least 30 characters, with pasting blocked | "Finally, participants were asked to write down reasons for their choice" (p. 152) | Length minimum; paste block |
| 9. Regret Scale | Five statements rated from 1 to 7 (exploratory) | Not in the original | New; after every original measure |
| 10. End form | Gambling frequency, influence of the feedback information on their choice, and demographics, each with "Prefer not to say"; optional feedback box | Not in the original | New |
| 11. Debrief | Explains what the study tested and that none of the gambles was played; clicking Finish saves the data and returns participants to Prolific with the completion code | Not described | New |

Several rules apply throughout:

| Rule | Detail | Difference from the original |
|---|---|---|
| No going back | Participants cannot return to earlier screens; for example, they cannot revise X after reading the feedback rule | On paper, participants could look back |
| No outcomes or bonuses | The gambles are never played, and every participant receives the same flat Prolific payment | Consistent with the original's hypothetical gambles; the original participants took part "as part of a course requirement" (p. 151) |
| Identical across conditions | Steps 1–3 and 7–11 are the same in every condition; only the feedback text (steps 4 and 6) and the correct answers to quiz items 4 and 5 differ | None |
| Data saving | Responses are saved after every screen, with the time spent on each screen and how often and how long the participant left the browser tab; if saving fails at the end, participants see their completion code and are asked to download and email their data | Not applicable |
| Bot detection | The Proof of Human tracker runs from consent to the end of the study. Its session ID is stored privately, and risk scores are retrieved from the vendor after data collection | None existed; the original was a supervised lab study |

The study takes about 6 minutes: in Pilot B, the median completion time was 5.7 minutes (range 2.3 to 10.6).

### Pilot B

Pilot B was run on Prolific with the final version of the study, recruiting US adults aged 18 or older without age or sex filters. Of 19 sessions, 3 were turned away by the device check, 2 declined consent, and 14 consented. Of those 14, 4 left before finishing, 3 of them during the comprehension quiz, and 10 completed the study; none of the completers met an exclusion criterion. Among the completers' 25 quiz attempts, item 4 was answered wrongly 11 times and item 5 9 times; both test the feedback rule, and 7 of the 10 completers needed more than one attempt to pass. The median completion time was 5.7 minutes (range 2.3 to 10.6).

After Pilot B, I made these changes: I set the bot-risk exclusion threshold at 50, set the expected study length at 6 minutes, restricted the age range to 18 to 25, and added a quota for equal numbers of men and women, removed the US residence filter. The gamble labels A and B, the combined matching and attractiveness screen, and the change to the debrief were made before Pilot B, so Pilot B tested them.

```{r}
#| label: pilot-b-data
#| include: false
# Pilot B's comprehension quiz. The chart counts the attempts of people who completed the study;
# the attempts table also shows those who left. Skipped if the Pilot B export is not there.
pilot_b_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", pilot_b_id)
have_pilot_b <- all(file.exists(file.path(pilot_b_dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))
if (have_pilot_b) {
  pb_participants <- read_csv(file.path(pilot_b_dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  pb_trials       <- read_csv(file.path(pilot_b_dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  pb_consented <- pb_trials |> filter(task == "consent", consented %in% TRUE) |> pull(participant_id)
  pb_completed <- pb_participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE, participant_id %in% pb_consented) |>
    pull(participant_id)
  pb_quiz      <- pb_trials |> filter(task == "comprehension")              # everyone who reached the quiz
  pb_quiz_done <- pb_quiz |> filter(participant_id %in% pb_completed)        # completers only
  quiz_items <- c(
    q1 = "1. Chance of winning $130 with Gamble A",
    q2 = "2. Chance of winning $X with Gamble B",
    q3 = "3. Would you know the outcome of the gamble you choose?",
    q4 = "4. If you choose Gamble A, would you know Gamble B's outcome?",
    q5 = "5. If you choose Gamble B, would you know Gamble A's outcome?")
  pb_item_errors <- tibble(item = names(quiz_items), label = unname(quiz_items)) |>
    mutate(wrong = map_int(item, ~ sum(!pb_quiz_done[[paste0(.x, "_correct")]] %in% TRUE)),
           attempts = nrow(pb_quiz_done), share = wrong / attempts)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: pilot-b-comprehension
#| eval: !expr have_pilot_b
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: !expr 'if (have_pilot_b) sprintf("Pilot B comprehension quiz: share of the %d quiz attempts by the %d participants who completed the study that answered each item wrongly. Items 4 and 5 test the feedback rule; their correct answers depend on the condition.", nrow(pb_quiz_done), n_distinct(pb_quiz_done$participant_id)) else ""'
pb_item_errors |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(unname(quiz_items)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = label)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1E6E76", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%d of %d", wrong, attempts)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.4, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, max(0.6, max(pb_item_errors$share) + 0.15)),
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
  labs(x = "Quiz attempts answering the item wrongly", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: pilot-b-attempts
#| eval: !expr have_pilot_b
# How many tries each participant needed (the quiz repeats until all five answers are correct).
pb_quiz |>
  count(participant_id, name = "attempts") |>
  mutate(outcome = if_else(participant_id %in% pb_completed, "Completed the study", "Did not complete")) |>
  count(Attempts = attempts, outcome) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = outcome, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  select(Attempts, any_of(c("Completed the study", "Did not complete"))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot B: number of quiz attempts per participant who reached the quiz.")
```

### Analysis plan

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

The analysis strategy, as close to the original as possible: data
cleaning rules, exclusion rules, covariates, and the model or test.
Original papers often do not spell this out; say where you had to make a
choice and what you chose.

**State the key analysis of interest explicitly.** That is the single
test your replication stands or falls on, and it must match your
preregistration. You can pre-specify additional analyses here too.
:::
-->

**Key analysis of interest.** I predict that more participants will choose the risky gamble (R) in the risky feedback condition than in the safe feedback condition. I will test this with a Pearson chi-square test of independence without continuity correction on the 2 × 2 table of feedback condition (risky vs. safe) by choice (R vs. S), with α = .05, two-sided. The effect size will be the difference in the proportion choosing R (risky feedback minus safe feedback) in percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval. In the original study this difference was 38 points [14, 63], χ²(1) = 7.88. The uncorrected test is the one that reproduces the original statistic from the original counts, so I will use it rather than a corrected test.

**Judging the replication.** Whether the 95% confidence interval excludes zero in the predicted direction, and whether it includes the original estimate of 38 points.

**Exclusions.** Participants removed by these exclusions will be replaced until 195 participants remain.

| Order | Rule | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Did not consent or did not complete the study | No complete data |
| 2 | Repeat sessions: sessions will be linked by Prolific ID. Each person's first completed session will be kept, and the person excluded if an earlier session had already reached the feedback instructions | A participant who has already seen a feedback rule is no longer naive to the manipulation |
| 3 | Any answer screen completed in under 300 ms: the matching and attractiveness screen, quiz, choice, strength of preference, reasons, Regret Scale and end form | Not humanly possible |
| 4 | A Proof of Human bot-risk score (0–100) of 50 or more, the threshold the vendor recommends for review, set after Pilot B and before preregistration. Participants without a score (tracker blocked or failed) will be kept, and their number reported | Likely a bot or AI agent |

**Secondary analyses.** These follow the remaining analyses of Experiment 1 (Zeelenberg et al., 1996, p. 152). Like the original, they will not be corrected for multiple comparisons, and they will be interpreted as secondary to the key test.

| Analysis | Test | Original result |
|---|---|---|
| Choice across all three conditions | χ²(2) on condition by choice | χ²(2) = 7.88, p < .02 |
| Risky feedback versus choice only | χ²(1) | χ²(1) = 1.93, ns (recomputed; listed as 2.18 in the paper) |
| Safe feedback versus choice only | χ²(1) | χ²(1) = 2.18, ns (recomputed; listed as 1.93 in the paper) |
| Risk preference across conditions | One-way ANOVA on risk preference, computed as choice (+1 for R, −1 for S) × (strength of preference − 0.5) | F(2, 75) = 3.46, p < .05 |
| Risk preference, risky versus safe feedback | Planned contrast using the error term from all three conditions, as in the original | t(75) = −2.63, p < .01 |
| Risk preference, risky feedback versus choice only | Planned contrast using the error term from all three conditions | t(75) = 1.44, ns (recomputed; listed as 1.19 in the paper) |
| Risk preference, safe feedback versus choice only | Planned contrast using the error term from all three conditions | t(75) = 1.19, ns (recomputed; listed as 1.44 in the paper) |
| Linear trend in risk preference | Linear contrast (risky feedback > choice only > safe feedback). With three conditions this is the same test as the risky-versus-safe contrast above (2.63² = 6.92), so it is not a separate result | F = 6.90, p < .01 |
| Matched X by condition | One-way ANOVA on X | F(2, 75) < 0.3 |
| Attractiveness of R versus S | Paired t-test on the two ratings | 6.71 versus 7.41, t(77) = −3.27, p < .01 |

**Exploratory analyses.** Because the original found that participants rated the gambles as not quite equally attractive after matching (p. 152), I will examine how well the matching worked: the number of participants who rated the two gambles exactly equally, and the mean difference between their ratings (R minus S), by condition; a logistic regression of choice on feedback condition (risky vs. safe) and the rating difference; and the key test repeated among participants who rated the gambles exactly equally. I will also examine whether trait regret-proneness, measured with the Regret Scale (Schwartz et al., 2002), strengthens the feedback effect, using a logistic regression of choice on the interaction between feedback condition and regret score, among participants in the risky and safe feedback conditions only. Any further analyses will be labelled as exploratory.


### Differences from the original study

<!--
::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every known difference in sample, setting, procedure, materials, and
analysis, one per row. Minimizing differences is the goal, but some
always remain. For each one, say whether it is expected to matter, based
on claims in the original article or later research on when the effect
does and does not appear. The rows below are the demo's real differences
and show the level of detail expected; replace them with yours.
:::
-->

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sample | 78 psychology undergraduates at the University of Amsterdam, taking part as a course requirement; age and gender not reported (p. 151) | 195 paid adults on Prolific, aged 18 to 25 and fluent in English, with equal numbers of men and women recruited through Prolific's quotas | Possibly. The age range moves the sample closer to the original's undergraduates. The original's sex ratio is unknown, so the equal split may differ from it; random assignment keeps the split similar across conditions, but it could shift how many participants choose the safe gamble overall. Online adult samples may also differ from students in a lab in attention and in familiarity with gambles. |
| Era | Mid-1990s | 2026 | Possibly; gambling is more familiar today. Gambling frequency is collected, so this can be examined. |
| Language | Probably Dutch (not stated) | English | Unknown |
| Setting | Separate cubicles, paper questionnaire (p. 151) | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own desktop or laptop | Possibly; attention may be lower online. The comprehension quiz, the speed rule and the repeat-session rule are intended to offset this. |
| Stakes | f130, about \$75 at the time; hypothetical (p. 151) | $130; hypothetical | Unlikely. The numbers are the same and the real value is roughly comparable today. |
| Wording | Questionnaire never published; only described in the paper (pp. 151–152) | Reconstructed from that description, in the second person | Possibly. The exact phrasing of the manipulation cannot be matched. |
| Feedback texts | The paper's description of the safe feedback condition contains an extra "only" | The risky and safe feedback texts are exact mirror images | Unlikely; this keeps the two conditions differing only in which gamble is named, and the original conditions were worded to be as similar as possible (M. Zeelenberg, personal communication, October 20, 2026). |
| Gamble display | A table (p. 151) | Two cards, Gamble A (risky) on the left and Gamble B (safe) on the right | Unlikely. The original questionnaire also labelled the gambles A and B (M. Zeelenberg, personal communication, October 20, 2026), so this matches it more closely than the paper's R and S. |
| Response format | Writing and circling on paper | Buttons for the ratings, choice and strength of preference; typed reasons | Unlikely; the scales (1–12) and wording are the same. |
| Comprehension quiz | None | Five questions before the choice, repeated until all are correct | Possibly; likely the most consequential addition. Participants should understand the feedback rule better. |
| Feedback rule on the choice screen | Presumably read once before choosing | Shown again on the choice screen | Possibly. |
| Reasons | Free writing | At least 30 characters, typed, with pasting blocked | Unlikely for the key test, which does not use the reasons. |
| Added measures | None | Regret Scale, gambling frequency, influence of the feedback information, and demographics, all after the choice | No; they come after the choice. |
| Assignment | Random, 26 per condition (p. 151) | Simple random assignment, so groups are approximately equal | No. |
| Navigation | Not described; a paper questionnaire would presumably allow looking back | No returning to earlier screens, so X cannot be revised after reading the feedback rule | Unlikely. |
| Exclusions | None reported | Did not consent or complete; repeat sessions; any answer screen under 300 ms; bot-risk score at or above the threshold | Unlikely; this removes invalid data, and every exclusion is reported with counts. |
| Analysis | χ² tests and risk-preference ANOVA and contrasts, judged on significance (p. 152) | The same tests, plus the difference in proportions with a 95% CI, judged on effect size | No for the key test. |

```{r}
#| label: phase1-data
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Loaded and excluded by read_phase(), under Key statistics, so Phase 1 and Phase 2 share one
# exclusion rule.
participants  <- phase1$participants
trials        <- phase1$trials
errors        <- phase1$errors
complete      <- phase1$complete
keep          <- phase1$keep
consented_ids <- phase1$consented_ids   # page loads where "I agree to participate" was clicked
```

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Every page load is a row in participants.csv, so the first step counts visits, including
# people who left at the consent screen and phones turned away (these have no condition).
funnel_levels <- c("Opened the study", "Consented", "Completed", "Passed exclusion criteria")
bind_rows(
  participants |> mutate(step = "Opened the study"),
  participants |> filter(participant_id %in% consented_ids) |> mutate(step = "Consented"),
  complete     |> mutate(step = "Completed"),
  keep         |> mutate(step = "Passed exclusion criteria")
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels),
         condition = factor(coalesce(unname(condition_labels[condition]), "No condition (turned away)"),
                            levels = c(condition_labels, "No condition (turned away)"))) |>
  count(step, condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  select(where(~ !is.numeric(.x) || sum(.x) > 0)) |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by feedback condition. Differences between conditions in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

```{r}
#| label: sample-text
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(sprintf("Of %d visits to the study, %d consented, %d completed the study and %d met the exclusion criteria.",
            nrow(participants), length(unique(consented_ids)), nrow(complete), nrow(keep)))
n_repeat <- length(phase1$repeat_ids)
repeats  <- sprintf("%d %s excluded as %s", n_repeat, if (n_repeat == 1) "was" else "were",
                    if (n_repeat == 1) "a repeat session" else "repeat sessions")
if (is.na(poh_exclude_at)) {
  cat(sprintf(" Of the completers, %s and %d for answering a screen in under %d ms (a participant can meet both).",
              repeats, length(phase1$too_fast_ids), min_screen_ms))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(" Of the completers, %s, %d for answering a screen in under %d ms and %d for a bot-risk score of %g or more (a participant can meet more than one).",
              repeats, length(phase1$too_fast_ids), min_screen_ms, length(phase1$bot_ids), poh_exclude_at))
}
if (is.null(phase1$poh)) {
  cat(" Bot-risk scores have not been fetched for these data yet, so that rule could not be applied.")
} else if (is.na(poh_exclude_at)) {
  cat(" No bot-risk threshold has been set yet, so nobody was excluded on bot-risk scores.")
}
if (!phase1$has_repeat_flags) cat(" These data were exported before repeat sessions were flagged, so that rule could not be applied; export again to apply it.")
if (nrow(keep) == 0) cat(" No participants remain for analysis yet, so the results below are empty.")
cat("\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: bot-risk
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Proof of Human bot-risk scores (0-100) among completers. poh_status comes from the participant
# document (what the tracker did); scores come from poh.csv, written by scripts/poh-scores.js.
bot <- complete |>
  transmute(participant_id, condition,
            poh_status = if ("poh_status" %in% names(complete)) as.character(poh_status) else NA_character_)
bot <- if (!is.null(phase1$poh)) {
  left_join(bot, phase1$poh |> transmute(participant_id, risk_score = as.numeric(risk_score),
                                         poh_error = as.character(poh_error)), by = "participant_id")
} else mutate(bot, risk_score = NA_real_, poh_error = NA_character_)

if (nrow(bot) > 0)
  bot |>
    mutate(Condition = factor(unname(condition_labels[condition]), levels = condition_labels)) |>
    group_by(Condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(Completed = n(), Scored = sum(!is.na(risk_score)),
              `Median score` = if (any(!is.na(risk_score))) median(risk_score, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_,
              `50 to 69` = sum(risk_score >= 50 & risk_score < 70, na.rm = TRUE),
              `70 or more` = sum(risk_score >= 70, na.rm = TRUE),
              Excluded = sum(participant_id %in% phase1$bot_ids), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = paste(
      "Proof of Human bot-risk scores among completers (0-100; higher means more likely a bot).",
      "The vendor suggests reviewing 50 to 69 and rejecting 70 or more.",
      if (is.na(poh_exclude_at)) "No exclusion threshold is set yet, so nobody is excluded on these scores."
      else sprintf("Completers scoring %g or more are excluded.", poh_exclude_at)))

# Completers without a score are kept; say why each one has none.
no_score <- bot |>
  filter(is.na(risk_score)) |>
  mutate(Reason = case_when(
    poh_status == "ready" & !is.na(poh_error) ~ paste("Report not available:", poh_error),
    poh_status == "ready"                     ~ "Scores not fetched yet (scripts/poh-scores.js)",
    poh_status == "off"                       ~ "Tracker off (no site key, or a test run)",
    poh_status == "failed_to_load"            ~ "Tracker blocked or failed to load",
    poh_status %in% c("loading", "no_session_id") ~ "Tracker never reported a session",
    TRUE                                      ~ "Not recorded (data predate the tracker)"))
if (nrow(no_score) > 0)
  no_score |> count(Reason, name = "Completers") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Completers without a bot-risk score, and why. They are kept in the analysis.")
```

```{r}
#| label: demographics
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Demographics come from the end form (task "end_survey"), stored as JSON in `response`.
# "Prefer not to say" counts as not given.
demo <- trials |>
  filter(task == "end_survey", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
  transmute(
    participant_id,
    age    = map_dbl(resp, ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x$age %||% NA))),
    gender = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$gender %||% NA))
  )

# Two separate statements, so both tables are shown.
if (nrow(demo) > 0)
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample.")
if (nrow(demo) > 0)
  demo |>
    count(Gender = coalesce(gender, "Not given")) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Gender of the analysed sample.")
```

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
choices <- trials |>
  filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  transmute(participant_id,
            condition = factor(condition, levels = names(condition_labels), labels = condition_labels),
            choice    = factor(choice, levels = c("risky", "safe"), labels = c("Gamble R (risky)", "Gamble S (safe)")))
risky <- risky_counts(phase1)

# A chi-square needs at least one participant in each row and each column; with a small
# pilot sample it often cannot be computed yet.
chisq_row <- function(tab, test, original_chi2) {
  ok <- nrow(tab) >= 2 && all(rowSums(tab) > 0) && all(colSums(tab) > 0)
  ct <- if (ok) suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE))
  tibble(Test = test, `Original χ²` = original_chi2,
         `χ²` = if (ok) sprintf("%.2f", ct$statistic) else "not computable yet",
         df = if (ok) as.character(ct$parameter) else "",
         p  = if (ok) format.pval(ct$p.value, digits = 2, eps = 0.001) else "",
         N  = sum(tab))
}
sub_tab <- function(conds) {
  tab <- table(Feedback = droplevels(choices$condition[choices$condition %in% conds]),
               Choice   = choices$choice[choices$condition %in% conds])
  tab
}

# Key test: risky feedback vs safe feedback, without continuity correction, so it matches the
# effect-size interval below (the uncorrected 2 x 2 chi-square is the same test as the
# two-proportion comparison) and the original's reported chi2(1) = 7.88.
key_tab <- sub_tab(condition_labels[c("risky_feedback", "safe_feedback")])
print(table(Feedback = choices$condition, Choice = choices$choice))

bind_rows(
  chisq_row(key_tab, "Key test: risky vs safe feedback", "7.88"),
  # Secondary tests the original also reports (p. 152). The overall test needs all three
  # conditions, so the empty ones are kept in the table (not dropped).
  chisq_row(table(Feedback = choices$condition, Choice = choices$choice),
            "All three conditions", "7.88 (df = 2)"),
  chisq_row(sub_tab(condition_labels[c("risky_feedback", "choice_only")]),
            "Risky feedback vs choice only", "1.93"),
  chisq_row(sub_tab(condition_labels[c("safe_feedback", "choice_only")]),
            "Safe feedback vs choice only", "2.18")
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Chi-square tests of gamble choice by feedback condition (no continuity correction). The first row is the key test; the others are the original's secondary tests. The paper lists the two comparisons with choice only as 2.18 and 1.93, in the opposite order; its counts and risk-preference means imply the assignment shown here.")
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test
is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with
the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the
original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original,
or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original
effect, are both informative and should be reported as such
(Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- diff_ci(original)
rep  <- diff_ci(risky)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Difference (risky − safe feedback)` = sprintf("%.0f points", 100 * estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.0f, %.0f]", 100 * ci_low, 100 * ci_high),
              p = ifelse(is.finite(p), format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001), "-")) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: difference in the percentage choosing the risky gamble, risky-feedback minus safe-feedback condition.")
} else {
  note("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least one analysed participant in both the risky-feedback and safe-feedback conditions.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of %.0f points. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    100 * orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and
your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing
in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect
came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary
    statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in
    the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on
    the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or
    it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as
    for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is
    possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as
    `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in
    columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}
    ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and
error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the
source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original
reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Percentage choosing the risky gamble (R) in each feedback condition: original study (Zeelenberg et al., 1996, Experiment 1, counts from Figure 1, p. 152) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = risky)
```

### Exploratory analyses

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory:
they were not planned, so they generate hypotheses rather than test
them.
:::

```{r}
#| label: secondary-original
#| eval: !expr have_data
# The original's secondary analyses (p. 152), run the same way here: the matched value X,
# the attractiveness ratings, and risk preference = (+1 risky / -1 safe) x (strength - 0.5).
# Each one says so instead of failing when there are too few participants (e.g. Pilot A).
in_keep <- function(t) trials |> filter(task == t, participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
# The attractiveness ratings are on the "matching" row since the two screens were combined; earlier
# data (Pilot A) have them on a separate "attractiveness" row. This reads either.
ratings_in_keep <- function() {
  trials |>
    filter(task %in% c("matching", "attractiveness"), participant_id %in% keep$participant_id,
           !is.na(attract_r), !is.na(attract_s))
}
by_condition <- function(df, var) {
  df |>
    mutate(Condition = factor(unname(condition_labels[condition]), levels = condition_labels)) |>
    group_by(Condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(N = n(), Mean = round(mean({{ var }}), 2), SD = round(sd({{ var }}), 2), .groups = "drop")
}
try_or_say <- function(expr, what) {
  tryCatch(expr, error = function(e) note(what, ": not enough data yet (", conditionMessage(e), ")."))
}

# (Each table and test below is its own top-level statement, so Quarto formats the tables.)
matching <- in_keep("matching")
attract  <- ratings_in_keep()
strength <- in_keep("preference_strength")

# 1. Matched value of X.
if (nrow(matching) > 0)
  by_condition(matching, matched_x) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Matched value of X (dollars) by condition. Original mean: %.2f (guilders), with no difference between conditions.",
                                   original_secondary$matched_x_mean))
if (nrow(matching) > 0) try_or_say(anova(lm(matched_x ~ condition, data = matching)), "ANOVA on X")

# 2. Attractiveness of the two gambles after matching (1-12).
if (nrow(attract) > 0)
  tibble(Gamble = c("R (risky)", "S (safe)"),
         Mean = round(c(mean(attract$attract_r), mean(attract$attract_s)), 2),
         Original = c(original_secondary$attract_r_mean, original_secondary$attract_s_mean)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Attractiveness ratings after matching (N = %d). Original: t(77) = -3.27, p < .01.",
                                   nrow(attract)))
if (nrow(attract) > 0)
  try_or_say(t.test(attract$attract_r, attract$attract_s, paired = TRUE), "Paired t-test")

# 3. Risk preference by condition, with the original's planned comparison (risky vs safe
# feedback) and linear trend (risky feedback > choice only > safe feedback).
if (nrow(strength) > 0)
  by_condition(strength, risk_preference) |>
    mutate(Original = unname(original_secondary$risk_pref_means[names(condition_labels)])) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Risk preference by condition (-11.5 = strongly safe, 11.5 = strongly risky), with the original's means.")
if (nrow(strength) > 0)
  try_or_say(anova(lm(risk_preference ~ condition, data = strength)), "ANOVA on risk preference")
# Planned contrasts, as in the original's t(75)s: each pair of conditions, all using the error
# term from all three conditions. Each difference is taken in the predicted direction (toward
# more risk-seeking with risky feedback), so a positive t supports the prediction. Risky vs safe
# feedback is also the linear trend (weights 1, 0, -1): the original's trend F = 6.90 is that t
# squared (2.63^2 = 6.92), so it is one test.
risk_contrasts <- function(d) {
  lv  <- names(condition_labels)
  n_c <- table(factor(d$condition, levels = lv))
  if (sum(n_c > 0) < 2) stop("needs participants in at least two conditions")
  fit <- lm(risk_preference ~ condition, data = d)
  if (df.residual(fit) < 1) stop("too few participants")
  mse <- sum(resid(fit)^2) / df.residual(fit)
  m   <- tapply(d$risk_preference, factor(d$condition, levels = lv), mean)
  pairs <- tribble(
    ~a,               ~b,              ~Contrast,                                 ~Original,
    "risky_feedback", "safe_feedback", "Risky - safe feedback (= linear trend)", "t(75) = 2.63 (reported as -2.63); trend F = 6.90",
    "risky_feedback", "choice_only",   "Risky feedback - choice only",           "t(75) = 1.44 (paper lists 1.19)",
    "choice_only",    "safe_feedback", "Choice only - safe feedback",            "t(75) = 1.19 (paper lists 1.44)"
  ) |> filter(n_c[a] > 0, n_c[b] > 0)   # a pair needs participants in both of its conditions
  pairs |>
    mutate(diff = as.numeric(m[a] - m[b]),
           t    = diff / sqrt(mse * (1 / as.numeric(n_c[a]) + 1 / as.numeric(n_c[b]))),
           df   = df.residual(fit),
           p    = format.pval(2 * pt(-abs(t), df), digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    transmute(Contrast, Difference = round(diff, 2), t = round(t, 2), df, p, Original)
}
if (nrow(strength) > 0)
  try_or_say(risk_contrasts(strength) |>
               knitr::kable(caption = paste(
                 "Planned contrasts on risk preference, each with the error term from all three conditions",
                 "(as in the original). Differences are in the predicted direction, so positive values support",
                 "the prediction. The original reports the first t with a minus sign and lists the two comparisons",
                 "with choice only in the opposite order; its means imply the values shown.")),
             "Risk-preference contrasts")
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-attractiveness
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: how well the matching worked, and whether that matters for the key effect.
# The ratings come before the feedback manipulation. Nobody is excluded on them; "matched" means
# Gamble R and Gamble S were rated exactly equally (difference 0, as Experiment 2 required).
att <- trials |>
  filter(task %in% c("matching", "attractiveness"), participant_id %in% keep$participant_id,
         !is.na(attract_r), !is.na(attract_s)) |>
  transmute(participant_id, att_diff = attract_r - attract_s) |>
  inner_join(trials |>
               filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
               transmute(participant_id, condition, risky = as.integer(choice == "risky")),
             by = "participant_id")
key_att <- att |>
  filter(condition %in% c("risky_feedback", "safe_feedback")) |>
  mutate(risky_feedback = as.integer(condition == "risky_feedback"))
matched_counts <- key_att |>
  filter(att_diff == 0) |>
  group_by(condition) |>
  summarise(risky = sum(risky), n = n(), .groups = "drop")

# 1. How often the two ratings were equal, and the mean difference, by condition.
if (nrow(att) > 0)
  att |>
    mutate(Condition = factor(unname(condition_labels[condition]), levels = condition_labels)) |>
    group_by(Condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Rated equally` = sum(att_diff == 0),
              `% rated equally` = round(100 * mean(att_diff == 0)),
              `Mean R minus S` = round(mean(att_diff), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: attractiveness of Gamble R minus Gamble S after matching, by condition (0 = rated equally). Original means: R 6.71, S 7.41.")

# 2. Covariate model (risky vs safe feedback): is the feedback effect still there once any
# leftover preference for R over S is taken into account?
# The model needs both choices in the data; when everyone chose the same gamble its estimates
# are meaningless (complete separation), so say so instead of printing them.
if (nrow(key_att) > 0 && n_distinct(key_att$risky) < 2)
  note("Logistic regression of choice on condition and rating difference: not computable yet (every participant chose the same gamble).")
if (nrow(key_att) > 0 && n_distinct(key_att$risky) == 2)
  try_or_say(summary(glm(risky ~ risky_feedback + att_diff, family = binomial, data = key_att))$coefficients,
             "Logistic regression of choice on condition and rating difference")

# 3. The key test repeated among participants who rated the two gambles exactly equally.
matched_r <- diff_ci(matched_counts)
if (nrow(key_att) > 0 && is.null(matched_r))
  note("Key test among equal raters: needs at least one equal rater in both the risky- and safe-feedback conditions.")
if (!is.null(matched_r))
  fmt_row("Equal raters only", matched_r) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: the key comparison among participants who rated Gamble R and Gamble S exactly equally.")
```

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-regret
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Exploratory: does trait regret-proneness strengthen the feedback effect? The Regret Scale
# (Schwartz et al., 2002) score is the mean of its five items (1-7, item 5 reversed; higher =
# more regret-prone). Logistic regression, among analysed participants in the risky- and
# safe-feedback conditions, of choosing the risky gamble on condition (risky feedback = 1), the
# regret score centred on its mean, and their interaction: a positive interaction means the
# feedback effect is larger for more regret-prone participants. The scale is answered after the
# choice, so the condition or the choice itself could have shifted it.
reg <- trials |>
  filter(task == "regret_scale", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  transmute(participant_id, regret_score = as.numeric(regret_score)) |>
  inner_join(trials |>
               filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
               transmute(participant_id, condition, risky = as.integer(choice == "risky")),
             by = "participant_id") |>
  filter(condition %in% c("risky_feedback", "safe_feedback"), !is.na(regret_score)) |>
  mutate(risky_feedback = as.integer(condition == "risky_feedback"),
         regret_c = regret_score - mean(regret_score))

regret_model <- function(d) {
  if (nrow(d) == 0) stop("no analysed participants in the risky- and safe-feedback conditions")
  if (n_distinct(d$risky) < 2) stop("every participant chose the same gamble")
  if (n_distinct(d$risky_feedback) < 2) stop("needs participants in both feedback conditions")
  fit <- suppressWarnings(glm(risky ~ risky_feedback * regret_c, family = binomial, data = d))
  est <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  # Estimates this large mean the groups are perfectly separated; they would not be meaningful.
  if (!fit$converged || nrow(est) < 4 || any(abs(est[, "Estimate"]) > 15))
    stop("the model cannot be estimated with these data (too few participants or perfect separation)")
  tibble(Term = c("Intercept (safe feedback, average regret score)", "Risky feedback (vs safe)",
                  "Regret score (per point, centred)", "Risky feedback x regret score"),
         `Log-odds` = round(est[, "Estimate"], 2), SE = round(est[, "Std. Error"], 2),
         z = round(est[, "z value"], 2),
         p = format.pval(est[, "Pr(>|z|)"], digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
         `Odds ratio [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", exp(est[, "Estimate"]),
                                         exp(est[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * est[, "Std. Error"]),
                                         exp(est[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * est[, "Std. Error"])))
}
if (nrow(reg) > 0)
  try_or_say(regret_model(reg) |>
               knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(paste(
                 "Exploratory: logistic regression of choosing the risky gamble on feedback condition (risky vs safe),",
                 "Regret Scale score (Schwartz et al., 2002; centred on its mean of %.2f) and their interaction (N = %d).",
                 "A positive interaction means the feedback effect grows with regret-proneness. The scale was answered",
                 "after the choice."), mean(reg$regret_score), nrow(reg))),
             "Regret Scale moderation")
if (nrow(reg) == 0)
  note("Regret Scale moderation: not enough data yet (no analysed participants in the risky- and safe-feedback conditions).")
```

```{r}
#| label: reported-measures
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Measures the Analysis plan reports but does not use to exclude anyone, by condition. Columns
# missing from older exports show as NA.
col_or_na <- function(df, col) if (col %in% names(df)) df[[col]] else rep(NA_real_, nrow(df))
per_task <- function(t, cols) {
  rows <- trials |> filter(task == t, participant_id %in% keep$participant_id)
  as_tibble(c(list(participant_id = rows$participant_id), setNames(lapply(cols, col_or_na, df = rows), cols)))
}
measures <- keep |>
  transmute(participant_id, condition, total_ms = col_or_na(keep, "total_ms")) |>
  left_join(trials |> filter(task == "comprehension", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
              group_by(participant_id) |> summarise(quiz_attempts = n(), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(trials |> filter(participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
              mutate(blur = col_or_na(pick(everything()), "blur_count")) |>
              group_by(participant_id) |> summarise(tab_aways = sum(blur, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop"),
            by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(per_task("reasons", c("paste_attempts", "too_short_attempts")), by = "participant_id") |>
  left_join(per_task("matching", "matched_x"), by = "participant_id")

if (nrow(measures) > 0)
  measures |>
    mutate(Condition = factor(unname(condition_labels[condition]), levels = condition_labels)) |>
    group_by(Condition, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(N = n(),
              `Median minutes` = round(median(as.numeric(total_ms), na.rm = TRUE) / 60000, 1),
              `% more than one quiz attempt` = round(100 * mean(quiz_attempts > 1)),
              `Mean tab-aways` = round(mean(tab_aways), 1),
              `% tried to paste` = round(100 * mean(paste_attempts > 0)),
              `% submitted too-short reasons` = round(100 * mean(too_short_attempts > 0)),
              `Median X` = median(matched_x),
              `X range` = if (n() > 0) paste(min(matched_x), "to", max(matched_x)) else "",
              .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Reported, not used to exclude anyone: completion time, quiz attempts, tab-aways, paste and too-short attempts on the reasons question, and the matched value of X, by condition.")
```
